name: Norwood Reaper

card.summary: Community nickname for male pattern hair loss advancing along the Norwood scale, used to frame hairline and hair-density preservation as part of keeping a youthful look.
card.note: Slang term, not a medical diagnosis; hair-loss treatments discussed alongside it carry their own side effects.

quick.overview:
The Norwood Reaper is looksmaxxing slang that personifies male pattern hair loss as a figure who "collects" a man's hair stage by stage, named after the Norwood scale that dermatologists use to grade it. Members of the community use it when discussing a receding hairline, temple recession or crown thinning, most often in relation to how hair affects facial appeal.

The term is a way of talking about a well-studied condition, androgenetic alopecia, which involves inherited sensitivity of scalp follicles to the hormone DHT. Because hair loss is common (roughly a third to half of men are affected by age 50 according to medical references), the Reaper features in threads about early detection, treatments, hairstyles and transplants.
quick.how: In practice the term appears in threads where users post before-and-after photos, ask whether a hairline is receding, or trade views on treatments that medical sources describe for male pattern hair loss: finasteride, topical minoxidil, and hair transplantation, along with shorter haircuts or other styling choices. Users describe watching for early signs in their teens and twenties and using the Norwood scale to place themselves on a stage.
quick.risks: The slang itself carries no risk, but threads under it often discuss prescription treatments, which have documented side effects and which some users say they hesitate to take. Some posters describe significant distress about hair loss; medical references describe male pattern hair loss as a moderately stressful condition that can lower body-image satisfaction, though most men cope and retain their sense of self.

lead: The Norwood Reaper is a looksmaxxing and wider online-forum personification of male pattern baldness (androgenetic alopecia). The name draws on the Hamilton-Norwood scale, the seven-stage grading system for male pattern hair loss, and on the figure of the Grim Reaper: the Reaper "takes" hair as a man moves from Norwood 1 toward Norwood 7. [1][2]

On looksmax.org the phrase is used for threads about hairline recession in young men, celebrity before-and-after comparisons, and questions about how to preserve or restore hair. Users connect hair to overall facial appeal, so hairline preservation is treated as a looks priority alongside skin, body fat and facial structure. [3][4]

The underlying condition is well documented in medical literature. It is driven by genetic sensitivity of scalp follicles to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), and standard treatments described by medical references include finasteride, minoxidil and hair transplantation. [2]

angle.text: The term itself is slang rather than a method. Users employ it to track their position on the Norwood scale and to discuss treatments and styling that medical sources describe for male pattern hair loss, with the goal of maintaining hair density and a youthful frame around the face.

infobox: looksmax.org, T Nation and other forums

paras: The Norwood Reaper is not a product or protocol. It is a shorthand for the progression of male pattern hair loss, usually used when someone notices recession at the temples or thinning at the crown. In forum usage it is typically a mock-ominous figure: a user "meets" the Reaper when recession begins, and a post may say the Reaper has "claimed" a person or celebrity. [3][5]
The term also appears outside looksmaxxing; users on the T Nation training forum use it in the same way when joking about their own thinning hair. [6]

sections.h: The Norwood scale behind the name
paras: James B. Hamilton described patterns of male baldness in 1951, and O'Tar Norwood revised and extended the scheme in 1975. The scale runs from stage 1 (no significant recession) through stage 7 (only a narrow horseshoe of hair around the back and sides), with stage 3 generally considered the first clinically significant stage, and 'A' variants for uniform front-to-back recession. [1]

Clinicians use the scale to assess severity, plan treatment and track change. It does not predict how quickly a given person will progress, and agreement between examiners on exact stage boundaries is described as moderate. [1]

sections.h: Causes and treatments in medical sources
paras: Medical references attribute male pattern hair loss to inherited sensitivity of scalp follicles to androgens, mainly DHT. Prevalence is commonly given as roughly 30 to 50 percent of men by age 50. [2]

Finasteride blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT, and increased scalp hair can appear within about three months; it is described as working better at the crown than at the front and temples. Minoxidil is a topical treatment whose mechanism is unclear, and combinations of finasteride, minoxidil and ketoconazole are described as more effective than any single agent. Hair transplantation by follicular unit extraction or strip harvesting is used in advanced cases. [2]

Threads using the term include a user in his early twenties describing temple recession despite a year of topical minoxidil and weekly hair oiling, who asked how to prevent further loss while expressing reluctance to take finasteride over side-effect concerns. [4]

Other threads compare celebrity photos taken years apart. One post about an actor describes the hairline as the main change in his appearance, while a reply notes that most men experience some hair loss eventually. [3]

Posts frequently express alarm about early recession, including threads by teenagers asking whether they are losing hair. Some replies recommend preventive prescription treatment at the first signs; others, in the same threads, treat hair loss more lightly. [5]

Medical references describe androgenetic alopecia as a moderately stressful condition that lowers body-image satisfaction in many men, who nonetheless usually cope and keep their sense of personality. [2] Forum language such as "death sentence" reflects the strong emotions some members attach to hairline loss, while other members point out how common it is.

No studies of the term or community framing itself were found. Clinical research on male pattern hair loss and its treatments (finasteride, dutasteride, minoxidil, transplantation) is extensive and is summarised in the medical references cited above. [2]

timeline.event: James B. Hamilton publishes a classification of male patterned baldness. [1]
O'Tar Norwood revises and expands the scheme into the seven-stage Norwood scale with Type A variants. [1]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the Reaper is both a joke and a genuine worry, with threads ranging from celebrity comparisons to personal hair-loss questions. [3][4]

claims.claim: Hair loss can drop a man's attractiveness by a whole tier
claims.believers: Posters argue that a receding hairline sharply changes how an otherwise attractive man is perceived, pointing to celebrity before-and-after photos. [3]
claims.experts: Medical references describe the condition as moderately stressful and linked to lower body-image satisfaction; no study cited here measures attractiveness tiers. [2]

claims.claim: Early prescription treatment at the first signs preserves the hairline
claims.believers: Some forum members advise starting finasteride at the first sign of recession, while others in the same threads weigh concerns about side effects. [4]
claims.experts: Medical references report that finasteride can increase scalp hair within months and works better at the crown than at the front and temples. [2]
